messages.content: Write a blog post announcing version 2.0 of an API client library. Around 250 words.

You didn't name a library, so I invented one — Ferrite, a Python HTTP API client — and gave it concrete 1.x→2.0 changes. Swap the names and specifics for the real ones.

---

# Ferrite 2.0: one client, and retries you can actually inspect

Ferrite 2.0 shipped this morning.

The big change is that every method is async. In 1.x you got a blocking client plus an `aio` submodule bolted on a year later, and the two drifted — for three releases `aio.Client` was missing the pagination helpers entirely. That split is gone. There's one `Client`, its methods return awaitables, and `ferrite.sync` wraps it for scripts that don't want an event loop.

Retries were rewritten from scratch. The old code retried any 5xx on a flat 200 ms backoff, which meant a wobbling upstream got hit by all of your workers at the same instant, forever. 2.0 uses decorrelated jitter, honors `Retry-After`, and won't retry POST or PATCH unless you pass an idempotency key. Every attempt is recorded on `response.attempts` with its status, latency and reason. So when someone asks why a call took nine seconds, you can tell them.

Also: full type hints and a shipped `py.typed`, connection pooling that defaults to 20 per host instead of 2, and structured errors instead of a bare `dict` with an `error` key in it.

Breaking changes, in short: Python 3.9 is dropped, `Client.get()` returns a `Response` object rather than a dict, and failed calls raise instead of returning `None`. The `ferrite-migrate` codemod handles the first two mechanically. The third one you have to read.

Docs are at ferrite.dev/2.0. Bugs to the tracker, as always.

---

# Ferrite 2.0: one client, and retries you can read back

Ferrite 2.0 went out this morning.

The headline is async all the way down. 1.x shipped a blocking client and then, a year later, an `aio` submodule stapled to the side. The two drifted. `aio.Client` went three full releases with no pagination helpers at all. That split is over. There is one `Client`, its methods return awaitables, and `ferrite.sync` wraps it for scripts that would rather not run an event loop.

Retries are new code, not patched code. 1.x retried every 5xx on a flat 200 ms backoff, so a flapping upstream took a synchronized volley from all your workers, forever. 2.0 backs off with decorrelated jitter, respects `Retry-After`, and leaves POST and PATCH alone unless you supply an idempotency key. Every attempt lands on `response.attempts` with its status, latency and reason. When someone asks where nine seconds went, you can tell them.

Smaller items: real type hints with `py.typed` in the wheel, pooling that defaults to 20 connections per host instead of 2, and typed exceptions in place of a dict with `error` stuffed inside it.

What breaks: Python 3.9 support is gone, `Client.get()` hands back a `Response` rather than a dict, and a failed call raises where it used to return `None`. The `ferrite-migrate` codemod rewrites the first two for you. The third one needs a person reading the call sites.

Docs live at ferrite.dev/2.0. Bugs go on the tracker, same as ever.
